title: MODULE 04 — Database Engineering and Backend Persistence

blocks.text: A backend application needs a reliable way to store information, retrieve it when required, and update it without corrupting existing data.
Imagine PrepSpaces has thousands of students using its learning platform. Each student can register, explore courses, enrol in multiple courses, track progress and complete lessons.

Where should this information be stored? How do we connect the backend to the database? What happens when two students try to enrol at the same time? How do we make sure that a student's enrolment is not accidentally duplicated?
These are the problems this module teaches you to solve.

You will learn how professional backend applications communicate with relational databases, use PostgreSQL for persistent storage, manage database relationships through JPA and Hibernate, execute safe transactions, and handle concurrent updates.
The module primarily uses **Java, Spring Boot, Spring Data JPA, Hibernate and PostgreSQL**.
By the end of this module, you should be able to:

items: Connect a Spring Boot application to PostgreSQL.
Design relational database schemas for real applications.
Understand how JPA and Hibernate work internally.
Map Java classes to database tables.
Model one-to-one, one-to-many and many-to-many relationships.
Manage transactions and maintain data consistency.
Apply database constraints to protect data integrity.
Identify and solve lazy-loading and N+1 query problems.
Manage schema changes through database migrations.
Prevent data conflicts when multiple users update records simultaneously.
Build a working course-enrolment API backed by a relational database.

blocks.text: Before working with database frameworks, you need to understand how information travels from a user's browser to a database and back.

A frontend application does not normally communicate directly with a production database. Instead, it sends an HTTP request to a backend API. The backend validates the request, performs the required business logic, communicates with the database and returns a response.

A relational database stores information in structured tables. Tables contain columns and rows, and relationships connect information across multiple tables.
For example, a learning platform might have separate tables for students, courses and enrolments.
Notice that student and course information is not repeatedly copied into the enrolment table. Instead, the table stores references to the relevant records.
**Primary Key (PK):** A column that uniquely identifies each record.
**Foreign Key (FK):** A column that references a record in another table.
**Relationship:** A logical connection between different tables.
**Normalization:** Organising database information to reduce unnecessary duplication and improve consistency.

Writing SQL for every database operation can become repetitive, particularly in applications containing dozens of entities.
Java applications commonly use Object-Relational Mapping (ORM) to map Java objects to relational database tables.
ORM allows you to work with database records using Java classes and objects.
For example, rather than manually inserting every student using SQL, you can create a Java `User` object and save it through a repository.
**JPA (Jakarta Persistence API)** is a specification that defines how Java applications should manage relational persistence.
**Hibernate** is an implementation of the JPA specification.
It performs the actual ORM work, including translating persistence operations into SQL, tracking managed entities and synchronizing their changes with the database.

items: `@Entity` tells JPA that this class represents a database entity.

blocks.text: Hibernate uses the entity mapping to interact with the corresponding database table.
**Persistence Context:** An environment in which the ORM manages entity instances and tracks their changes.
**Entity Lifecycle:** Entities can be transient, managed, detached or removed.
**Dirty Checking:** Hibernate detects changes to managed entities and can generate the required SQL updates when the persistence context is flushed.
**EntityManager:** JPA's primary interface for managing entities and interacting with the persistence context.
**Why this lesson matters:** You need to understand what JPA and Hibernate actually do instead of treating them as magic tools that automatically save data.
Entity mapping connects Java classes and their fields to database tables and columns.

sections.title: Lesson 6 — One-to-One, One-to-Many and Many-to-Many Relationships

blocks.text: Real applications contain related data. JPA provides relationship annotations that represent these connections.
You must understand these relationships before designing larger database systems.
One record in one table is associated with one record in another table.
**Example:** One user has one student profile.
You will also learn how foreign keys and unique constraints enforce a true one-to-one relationship in the database.
One record is associated with multiple records in another table.
**Example:** One instructor can create multiple courses.
The many side generally owns the foreign key:
You will understand the difference between owning and inverse sides of a relationship.
Multiple records in one table can be associated with multiple records in another table.
**Example:** Students can enrol in multiple courses, and each course can have multiple students.
A many-to-many relationship typically uses a junction table.
Each enrolment connects one user to one course. Multiple enrolment records connect students and courses.

**Why this lesson matters:** Correct relationships prevent duplicated information and provide a foundation for complex application data.

sections.title: Lesson 7 — Repository Patterns and Database Queries

blocks.text: A backend needs a clean way to retrieve, insert, modify and delete database information.
Spring Data JPA provides repository abstractions that reduce repetitive database-access code.
A repository acts as an interface between your application and its persistence layer.
Instead of writing SQL for every basic operation, you can define a repository interface.
Spring Data JPA generates the implementation for supported repository methods.
Spring Data JPA can generate queries based on method names.
You will also learn when repository method naming is insufficient.
JPQL operates on entities and their properties, rather than directly using database table and column names.
**Why this lesson matters:** A well-structured persistence layer keeps database access organised and makes backend services easier to maintain.
One of the most important topics in backend engineering is transaction management.
A transaction groups multiple database operations into one logical unit of work.

What happens if the enrolment record is created successfully, but updating the seat count fails?
The database could end up in an inconsistent state.
ACID describes four important transaction properties.
| Atomicity   | All operations succeed or the transaction is rolled back                                                  |
| Consistency | Transactions maintain database rules and integrity                                                        |
| Isolation   | Concurrent transactions are controlled to prevent invalid interference                                    |
| Durability  | Committed changes persist even after a system failure, subject to the database's durability configuration |
A transaction boundary defines where a transaction begins and ends.
In Spring Boot, you commonly use `@Transactional` at the service layer.
In a real implementation, the service would also validate the student, course, duplicate enrolment and course capacity within the appropriate transactional operation.

blocks.text: **Important:** A transaction does not automatically make an application correct. You must choose suitable boundaries, constraints and concurrency controls.

sections.title: Lesson 9 — Database Constraints and Data Integrity

blocks.text: Data integrity means ensuring that stored information remains correct, valid and consistent.
Application-level validation is important, but relying only on backend validation is not enough. The database must also protect important rules.
Ensures each record has a unique identifier.
Ensures that a reference points to an existing record.
Prevents a column from accepting null values.
Ensures that a value satisfies a condition.
Provides a default value when no value is supplied.
A student should not be able to enrol in the same course twice.

**Why this lesson matters:** The database is the final enforcement layer for critical data rules, especially when multiple application requests are running concurrently.

sections.title: Lesson 10 — Lazy Loading, Eager Loading and the N+1 Problem

blocks.text: This lesson introduces an important performance problem that frequently appears in applications using ORM frameworks.
You can write perfectly valid JPA code and still create hundreds of unnecessary database queries.
Lazy loading means related data is generally retrieved only when the relationship is accessed.
When the user is initially retrieved, Hibernate does not necessarily retrieve all associated enrolments.
It retrieves them when they are accessed while the required persistence context is available.
Eager loading means that related information is required as part of loading the entity.
The exact SQL strategy used depends on the relationship and Hibernate's loading plan. Eager loading does not necessarily mean one SQL join.
The initial query retrieves all students:
Then the application accesses the enrolments of every student.
Hibernate may execute another query for each student:
This produces one initial query plus additional queries for each student.
One suitable fetch query for the required data
Illustrative query counts for 100 students and their enrolments. The actual number depends on the fetching strategy.
How to solve the N+1 problem
**JOIN FETCH:** Retrieves related information using a JPQL fetch join.
**Entity Graph:** Defines which relationships should be retrieved for a particular query.
**Batch Fetching:** Retrieves related records in batches rather than executing a separate query for every entity.
**DTO Projections:** Retrieves only the data needed for the API response.
**Database Query Analysis:** Uses SQL logs and performance monitoring to identify unnecessary queries.
You will also understand the problems caused by accessing lazy relationships after the persistence context has closed, including `LazyInitializationException`.
**Why this lesson matters:** Database performance becomes critical as the number of users and records increases.

How do you safely update the database structure without destroying existing information?
This is where database migrations are used.
A migration is a controlled and versioned change to the database schema or data.
Rather than manually changing the production database, you maintain migration files in your application repository.

ALTER TABLE users
ADD COLUMN phone_number VARCHAR(20);
When Flyway runs, it records which migrations have already been applied and executes pending migrations in the correct order.
**Versioned Migrations:** Changes are recorded using ordered migration files.
**Migration History:** Tracks which changes have already been applied.
**Schema Evolution:** Allows database structures to evolve as the application develops.
**Rollback Strategy:** Not every migration can be safely reversed automatically. You must plan recovery or forward-fix procedures.
**Data Migration:** Updates existing records when the structure or meaning of data changes.
You will learn the fundamentals of:

items: Development, staging and production migration workflows.

blocks.text: Avoid allowing Hibernate to automatically modify production database schemas with `ddl-auto=update`.
For controlled environments, prefer versioned migrations and validate that the application's entity mappings match the deployed schema.
**Why this lesson matters:** Professional applications need predictable, reviewable database changes across multiple environments.
Concurrency becomes important when multiple users perform operations at the same time.
Imagine a course has only one available seat.
Two students click the Enrol button at nearly the same moment.
Both requests check the available seat count and see one seat remaining.
Without appropriate protection, both students might successfully enrol.
You will study problems such as:
Optimistic locking assumes that conflicts are relatively uncommon.
It uses a version field to detect whether a record has been changed since it was read.
When Hibernate updates the entity, it checks the version.
If another transaction has already updated it, the operation can fail with an optimistic locking conflict.
The application can then handle the conflict instead of silently overwriting newer data.
Pessimistic locking prevents other transactions from modifying a selected record while the lock is held.
This is useful in operations that require stronger control over shared data.
However, excessive locking can reduce throughput or cause deadlocks.
Some concurrency problems can be prevented by making a condition and update part of the same SQL statement.

UPDATE courses
SET available_seats = available_seats - 1
WHERE id = 101
AND available_seats > 0;
The backend checks the number of affected rows to determine whether a seat was successfully reserved.
A transaction can then create the corresponding enrolment record. Both operations must succeed together.
| Pessimistic locking | Operations requiring exclusive access  |
| Atomic SQL updates  | Conditional counters and reservations  |
**Why this lesson matters:** A backend must remain correct even when hundreds of users access and modify the same information simultaneously.

# **5. Assignment — Design Database Entities for a Learning Platform**
Design a relational database and implement transactional operations for a learning platform similar to PrepSpaces.
A learning platform allows users to register, browse courses, enrol in courses, track learning progress and complete modules.
Your task is to design a database that supports these operations while maintaining data consistency and performance.
Explain why each relationship is needed.
Use Spring Data JPA repositories and a service-layer architecture.
Demonstrate how your application responds when an operation fails midway.
Identify at least one possible N+1 query problem and fix it.
Implement either optimistic or pessimistic locking for an operation that can be affected by concurrent updates.
Explain why your selected strategy is appropriate.
Your assignment must contain the database schema, entity relationship diagram, Java entity classes, repository interfaces, service implementations, REST controllers, migrations and automated tests.
After completing the practical lab and assignment, you should be able to reason about problems like these:
**Challenge 1 — Duplicate enrolment:** Two identical enrolment requests arrive simultaneously. How will you guarantee that only one enrolment is created?
**Challenge 2 — Limited course seats:** A course has one seat remaining, but two students try to enrol. How will you prevent over-enrolment?
**Challenge 3 — Slow API:** Your course API retrieves 500 students and their enrolments, executing hundreds of unnecessary SQL queries. How will you diagnose and optimise it?

**Challenge 4 — Database schema change:** Your live platform has thousands of users. You need to add a new mandatory column without breaking the existing application. How will you migrate the data safely?
**Challenge 5 — Partial failure:** An enrolment record is saved, but the course seat count is not updated. How will you guarantee consistency?
These challenges connect the concepts in this module to real backend engineering work.

By the end of Module 04, you will understand how a professional backend application persists information and protects it from corruption, duplication, inconsistent updates and unnecessary database operations.

You will move beyond simply connecting a database to an application. You will understand how to design data models, manage persistence, write efficient queries, coordinate transactions and handle concurrent users.
**Your final objective:** Be able to design and implement a reliable PostgreSQL-backed persistence layer for a real-world Spring Boot application, rather than simply performing basic CRUD operations.
